name: The McGurk Effect
statement: What you see a mouth doing changes what you hear it say.
statementAccent: changes what you hear it say
meaning: A perceptual illusion in which visual information about a talker's mouth alters what a listener hears. When the sound 'ba' is dubbed onto video of a face mouthing 'ga,' most people report hearing 'da' — a third syllable matching neither the sound nor the lips. Speech perception is not purely acoustic: the brain fuses what the ears pick up with what the eyes see.
mechanism: The effect is a demonstration of multisensory integration. When the auditory and visual speech cues conflict, the brain does not simply pick one but fuses them, producing a compromise percept that reconciles the incompatible place-of-articulation information — the sound of 'ba' and the sight of 'ga' meeting in the middle as 'da.' The visual channel is recruited automatically as part of ordinary speech perception, which is why seeing a speaker's face aids understanding in noise.

examples.text: Hearing the sound 'ba' while watching a face mouth 'ga' produces the perception of 'da' — the canonical demonstration from the original 1976 study.
Unlike many illusions, the McGurk effect persists even when you know the sound and video are mismatched and understand exactly how it works — knowledge does not dispel the percept.
The effect is part of why poorly dubbed film, with lips out of sync with the audio, feels perceptually wrong — the mismatched visual speech interferes with what is heard.

variants.name: The ventriloquist effect
variants.text: A related audiovisual illusion in which vision captures the perceived location of a sound, rather than its content — the source seeming to come from a moving mouth, as with a dummy.

variants.name: Audiovisual speech perception
variants.text: The broader phenomenon the effect belongs to, in which seeing a speaker's face routinely aids and shapes the perception of speech, especially in noise.

whyItMatters: It is a striking and much-replicated demonstration that perception is multisensory — that we hear with our eyes as well as our ears. It reshaped the understanding of speech perception as an integrated audiovisual process and remains a workhorse for studying how the brain combines information across the senses.

working.text: treat speech perception as audiovisual, so what a listener sees a mouth doing can change what they report hearing.
recognise that seeing a speaker's lips genuinely aids comprehension when the sound is degraded, since the brain integrates the two.

working.lead: Do not expect to think it away
working.text: know that understanding the illusion does not switch it off — the fusion is automatic and persists despite knowledge.

limits: The effect is robust and widely replicated, but its strength varies substantially with the individual, the language, the developmental stage, and the specific stimulus. Cross-language findings are genuinely mixed: early work reported a weaker effect in Japanese listeners, but later studies found the reverse under different conditions, so speaker and stimulus differences may matter more than native language. Susceptibility is present in infancy and generally strengthens through childhood, and some individuals show strong fusion while others show almost none. The variation is in magnitude, not in whether the effect exists.
misreadings: It is not simply that vision helps hearing — the seen mouth can override the sound and produce a syllable that was never spoken. And the claim that some language groups reliably show a weaker effect is an oversimplification; the cross-language evidence is mixed, with stimulus and individual differences often outweighing language.
origin: Discovered accidentally and reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 'Hearing lips and seeing voices,' Nature 264:746-748 (1976), while they were studying infant speech perception.

sources.text: McGurk effect, Wikipedia. — the illusion, the audiovisual-fusion mechanism, the 1976 origin, and the cross-language variation.
MacDonald, "Hearing Lips and Seeing Voices: the Origins and Development of the McGurk Effect," Multisensory Research (2018), PubMed. — the accidental discovery and the effect's history.
